title: The Future of Everything Is Emergent
author: Patrick Dempsey
summary: Patrick Dempsey uses Airbnb's announced AI travel agent, which will build a personalized interface in real time from a library of travel components, as evidence that software is moving from predetermined interfaces to ones assembled around each user's intent. He lays out a progression from Google's links, to ChatGPT's synthesized answers, to systems that understand intention, assemble an experience and help the user act, combining generative AI, agentic AI and generative UI. A personal story about a missed technician notification illustrates his central idea that what begins as an innovation becomes an expectation, and its absence then feels like failure. He applies this to education, arguing that the gap between students' experience of the real world and of institutions built on predetermined courses, schedules and learning management systems is already nearly unbridgeable. The post ends by asking readers whether they would use a site designed like Amazon's original homepage today, implying institutions risk looking equally outdated.
points: Airbnb's planned agent assembles a bespoke interface per trip, which Dempsey reads as a shift from navigating designed interfaces to having them generated around intent.
He distinguishes generative AI that produces content, agentic AI that pursues goals and takes actions, and generative UI that composes interfaces for the moment.
His core principle is that innovations harden into expectations, so absence of the new experience reads as something being broken.
Learning management systems and fixed course structures already feel unintelligible to students used to personalized technology elsewhere.
He frames education's predetermined design of courses, schedules and assessments as the opposite of where the wider world is heading.
quotes: In other words, while Google in its original form allowed us to search for answers, AI uses answers to shape what happens next.
We’re moving toward a world where technology shifts from making the world searchable to making it answerable.
What Airbnb is building is a system that takes your intention, understands the context, assembles an interface and experience appropriate to the problem, and helps you act.

And when that expectation is not the experience, I have been trained to assume something has gone wrong. The tech could literally be standing outside my house and, as far as I’m concerned, the appointment isn’t happening.
What begins as an innovation eventually becomes an expectation. And once it becomes an expectation, its absence feels like a failure.

The distance between how students experience the “real world” and how they experience education is already nearly unbridgeable. There is nothing about modern LMSs, for example, that makes any sense with respect to the state of the technology we use in any other context (besides maybe government websites . . .).
We’ve organized education around predetermined everything. Courses, schedules, assignments, assessments, learning pathways. We build the experience and students navigate it.
context: Search is giving way to systems that use answers to shape the next action.
The shift is from searchable information to answerable, actionable systems.
Airbnb's agent is the example of an interface assembled around a user's goal.
A routine service failure shows how technology resets what people expect.
Dempsey's central claim is that expectations ratchet upward once an innovation lands.
He argues education's technology already looks outdated against students' everyday experience.
Predetermined course design is set against a world moving toward on-demand assembly.
